corpusSources.title: Mexica (Aztec) Mythology and Ritual Traditions
corpusSources.creator: Nahua authors, ritual specialists, communities, and colonial-period textual witnesses
corpusSources.firstAppearance: Pre-contact traditions with colonial-period textual and material witnesses
corpusSources.continuityUnit: Source-specific corpus; distinguish Mexica from broader Nahua and other Mesoamerican traditions
corpusSources.distinctiveContribution: Layered heavens and underworlds, calendrical time, divine forces and embodiments, sacred warfare, offerings, cosmic maintenance, world ages, migration memory, place-based identity, and ritual-political authority.
corpusSources.scopeNote: Use specialist, community-aware, archaeological, and primary textual sources. Avoid treating 'Aztec mythology' as a closed pantheon roster or merging it with Maya, generic Mesoamerican, or commercial adaptation categories.

corpusSources.continuityUnit: Retold base game plus dated official pantheon and god-pack expansions

corpusSources.scopeNote: Commercial game adaptation, not evidence for the source traditions it represents. Version-stamp pantheon rosters, expansions, balance changes, and names; analyze Greek, Egyptian, Norse, Atlantean, Chinese, Japanese, and Mexica/Aztec adaptation layers separately.

omissions: Most named Olympians and Titans not needed for this bounded pass

Regional variants; vase/iconographic evidence; lyric, Hellenistic, Roman, and Byzantine receptions
Tragedies and epic cycles beyond the named works, except the Oedipus at Colonus locator explicitly noted in two records
uncertainties: Ancient Greek myth has variant genealogies, motives, divine jurisdictions, and characterizations; this pass preserves selected-witness provenance rather than reconciling them.
'Pseudo-Apollodorus' is conventional modern attribution for the Library; the record retains the work title rather than treating authorship as certain.
Some modern comparison IDs are intentionally blank where a mapping would distort a source-native ontology.
sources.evidence_basis: Every character and relationship is tied to a primary-text locator in a scholarly digital repository. URLs identify the edition/repository; locators identify the precise book, hymn, or line range.

supports: Hesiodic Theogony is a named witness in the pass and illustrates the primary-text repository basis.

sources.title: Ancient Greek Mythology

sources.coverage_rule: Major named divine, primordial, heroic, royal, nymph, and monster agents materially active in the selected witnesses, plus figures needed to retain distinct ontological or narrative categories. The pass is representative and foundational, not all names in Greek literature.

omissions: Tablet XII is excluded: it is a separate/sequel-like tablet in the Standard Babylonian series and not used to add a second Enkidu-underworld episode.

Collective or unspecified actors such as the Elders of Uruk, the hunter/trapper, Utnapishtim’s wife, the Scorpion Man’s wife, and the great gods as an unnamed collective are deliberately not nodes; the elders are retained as a source term.
Fragmentary readings and portions of tablets lost in the manuscript record are not reconstructed as new character actions.
uncertainties: The Standard Babylonian poem survives only in a composite scholarly reconstruction from fragmentary manuscripts; a cited tablet/line is a reconstructed text location, not a claim that one intact tablet preserves every word.

Names and divine identities have variant spellings/transliterations (for example, Gilgameš/Gilgamesh, Ištar/Ishtar, Uta-napišti/Utnapishtim, and Enlil/Ellil). Display labels follow cautious conventional English with aliases.
Old Babylonian material has a different textual organization and wording. It is cited only to document the distinction, never as a replacement for a missing Standard Babylonian line.

sources.continuity_scope: A bounded, tradition-level orientation pass for the broader Sanskrit Mahābhārata tradition, not a replacement text or a universal canon. Primary textual orientation is limited to the Adi Parva frame (Ugraśravas Sauti and Śaunaka) and two Vana Parva embedded narratives (Nala–Damayantī and Sāvitrī–Satyavān), using Kisari Mohan Ganguli’s public-domain English translation as an accessible, non-critical translation witness. Oxford Academic scholarship establishes that the Mahābhārata is best approached as a plurality of oral, textual, and performative traditions. This pass is distinct from SRC-277 BORI Critical Edition and SRC-278 Bhagavad Gītā; it neither transfers their claims nor merges their character records.
work_or_witnesses: Mahābhārata, Adi Parva, Section I and Pauloma Parva, Section IV — narrative frame in the Ganguli translation witness
Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Nalopākhyāna, Sections LIII–LVII — Nala–Damayantī witness in the Ganguli translation
Mahābhārata, Vana Parva, Pativratā-māhātmya, Sections CCXLI–CCXLII — Sāvitrī–Satyavān witness in the Ganguli translation
Oxford Bibliographies in Hinduism: Pamela Lothspeich, “Mahābhārata in Hindu Tradition,” and Simon Brodbeck, “Mahābhārata”
BORI official Critical Edition overview, used only to distinguish SRC-277
sources.coverage_rule: Include six named individuals needed to make the umbrella scope legible without duplicating SRC-277’s large BORI cast or SRC-278’s Gītā dialogue: Ugraśravas Sauti and Śaunaka for the Sanskrit textual recital frame; Nala and Damayantī for the Nalopākhyāna; and Sāvitrī and Satyavān for the Pativratā-māhātmya. These are not an attempt at a comprehensive epic dramatis personae, a cross-tradition identity ledger, or a claim that these stories carry the same authority, form, or meaning in every living, regional, devotional, or performance context.
omissions: The 49-character BORI Critical Edition cohort in SRC-277, including its principal Kuru-war cast, and the four-character Bhagavad Gītā cohort in SRC-278. The same names, where they appear elsewhere, must never be identity-merged or claim-transferred across source IDs.

All other Sanskrit Mahābhārata figures, including hundreds of genealogy, war, pilgrimage, didactic, divine, rākṣasa, nāga, and embedded-tale figures; collective categories and unindividualized figures remain terms/context.

Regional recensions; vernacular retellings; oral, sung, ritual, theatrical, dance, visual, television, film, comic, game, and other performance/adaptation traditions; commentarial, sectarian, and devotional layers; South and Southeast Asian traditions not represented by these witnesses.
Harivaṃśa and other associated texts; any single manuscript, printed Sanskrit edition, or critical edition beyond the narrow boundary statement; translations other than the declared Ganguli witness.

Claims about contemporary Hindu belief or practice; fixed pan-Indian caste/varna, gender, sexuality, disability, ethnicity, race, political, legal, historical, or moral norms; and colonial-era translation language as a transparent substitute for Sanskrit categories.
uncertainties: Oxford scholarship describes the Mahābhārata as a narrative tradition with oral, textual, and performative versions. Accordingly, this pass does not treat a single printed text, translation, or critical edition as the whole tradition or as normatively superior.

Ganguli’s nineteenth-century English translation is a valuable accessible translation witness, but its Victorian diction, transliteration, selection, and section labels are not Sanskrit text, not a BORI Critical Edition translation, and not neutral language for caste, gender, sacred, or social categories. All Ganguli locators are marked as translation-witness locators only.

The BORI Critical Edition is intentionally separate in SRC-277. Its critical constitution, manuscript method, and character records cannot establish the content of this umbrella pass, and this umbrella cannot settle textual-critical questions or make a ‘most authentic’ claim.
The Bhagavad Gītā is an embedded, separately scoped sacred dialogue in SRC-278; its characters and terms are not re-recorded here merely because it occurs inside the epic.

Nala–Damayantī and Sāvitrī–Satyavān are selected only as bounded Sanskrit embedded narratives. Their later devotional, gendered, regional, performance, translation, and modern political receptions require their own witnesses and specialists.

Sanskrit terms remain source-native and context-dependent. Deva, asura, rākṣasa, nāga, dharma, karma, tapas, mantra, astra, vrata, varṇa, boon, curse, and kinship practices must not be flattened into D&D-style races, classes, alignments, mechanics, or universal social categories.
sources.evidence_basis: The declared Ganguli translation supplies precise narrative section locators for the six selected figures and their three limited relationships. Oxford Academic supplies the scholarly rationale for a tradition-level, plural rather than single-text approach and notes the frame, eighteen-parvan structure, and subsidiary-tale breadth. BORI’s official page is cited only to enforce separation from SRC-277. No Wikipedia, fan source, unexamined vernacular adaptation, or claim about living practice is used as evidence.

sources.coverage_rule: No individual characters are included. The accessible official Standard 5E core page and character sheet identify player-character roles, covenants, Mythic Europe, magical Arts, and mechanics, but do not offer a stable claim-level profile for a named dramatic individual. Houses, Hermetic roles, magic Arts, covenants, creatures, medieval places, history, and rules remain terms/context unless an individual named dramatic character is directly profiled by the selected witness.
omissions: All named individuals, historical people, saints, legendary beings, deities, sample magi, and story characters, because the selected accessible Standard 5E core witness does not provide claim-level dramatic profiles.
All claims from fifth-edition sourcebooks, adventures, tribunals, Realms of Power, Houses of Hermes, novels, fan material, and home sagas, even where marketed as usable with Fifth Edition.
All first- through fourth-edition material and all Definitive Edition Expanded Core Rulebook material; compatibility or shared terminology does not merge editions/products.
All real-world medieval historical, religious, legal, ethnic, geographic, or cultural claims not independently supported by appropriate historical scholarship.
uncertainties: Mythic Europe blends historical and fantastical material for play. Its fictional depiction is not evidence about medieval Europe, Christianity, Islam, Judaism, other religions, historical communities, or historical people.

The Standard 5E product page says older sourcebooks are generally usable with the newest edition, but that is a compatibility statement, not a source hierarchy, continuity merger, or retcon resolution for this audit.

The official errata page includes corrections for the Fifth Edition Second Printing and was last updated in February 2024. It is a maintenance boundary; unexamined individual errata changes are not imported as terms or character claims.

Atlas lists Ars Magica Definitive Edition as a separate expanded core product with a release date of TBD. No Definitive Edition content, pagination, or changes are inferred into the selected Standard 5E record.

The current CC BY-SA 4.0 open license covers the text of Fifth Edition books, not their trade dress, graphic design, artwork, cartography, or logos unless specified. This audit records that copyright/license boundary and makes no legal determination about particular downstream works.
Magic, supernatural beings, and fictionalized religious material may be central to play. They are source-native fantasy constructs, not claims about living belief or real supernatural practice.

Journey to the West and Investiture of the Gods are excluded as primary evidence for this source.

sources.continuity_scope: A deliberately bounded, source-critical pass across three colonial-period witnesses to Nahua/Mexica knowledge: the 1577 Florentine Codex (books 1–4, 8, and 12 at the cited folios), the Nahuatl Leyenda de los Soles preserved in the Códice Chimalpopoca (UNAM edition), and the pictorial Códice Boturini/Tira de la Peregrinación (INAH edition). These are not transparent records of a single pre-contact canon: they are colonial manuscripts and editions, with distinct authorship, languages, media, places, editorial histories, and purposes. The pass distinguishes (rather than merges) pre-contact practices inferable only through such witnesses; colonial transcription and translation; Mexica/Tenochtitlan-specific material; broader or regional Nahua materials; contemporary community practice and reconstruction; and commercial game/adaptation portrayals.

work_or_witnesses.work: Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España (Florentine Codex), Ms. Mediceo Palatino 218–20
work_or_witnesses.edition: Digital Florentine Codex, Getty Research Institute, 2023; manuscript completed in 1577, with Nahuatl and Spanish columns and named Indigenous/Nahua collaborators in the catalogue citation.

work_or_witnesses.work: Leyenda de los Soles in Códice Chimalpopoca
work_or_witnesses.edition: Primo Feliciano Velázquez, trans.; Miguel León-Portilla, pref.; 3rd ed., UNAM Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas, 1992; digitized 2019. This Spanish translation is used only with page-specific attribution to the colonial Nahuatl witness.

work_or_witnesses.work: Códice Boturini / Tira de la Peregrinación
work_or_witnesses.edition: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia digital edition, 2015. A colonial pictorial manuscript; INAH identifies 22 sheets and a migration account from Aztlan toward the foundation of Mexico-Tenochtitlan.

sources.coverage_rule: Include only the fifteen individually named agents who materially speak, direct, act, or undergo a narratively consequential action in these exact passages: Florentine Codex book 3 fols. 1v–2v; Florentine Codex book 12 fol. 14v; and Leyenda de los Soles pp. 120–122. The contextual term set is restricted to exact witness-grounded vocabulary in the cited Florentine and Boturini passages. Generic teotl, unnamed ritual participants, the Centzonhuitznahuah collective, captive persons, places, institutions, calendar signs, artifacts, and categories are not character nodes. No figure is added merely because later scholarship, revival, a game, or a popular pantheon list associates it with the tradition.
omissions: All unnamed persons, collectives, offices, places, calendrical signs, offerings, iconographic motifs, and ritual embodiments
The many named figures outside the specified folios/pages, including the majority of each witness
Maya, Mixtec, and other Mesoamerican traditions; regional Nahua witnesses not named above; and modern Nahua community practices
Modern reconstruction, academic synthesis beyond the bounded witnesses, films, novels, comics, games, and other adaptations
uncertainties: A colonial witness does not directly disclose an unchanged pre-contact practice; its compilation, transcription, translation, and editorial framing must remain visible.
The terms teotl and ixiptla/ixiptlahtli are polysemous and context-sensitive; English 'god', 'idol', 'image', 'impersonator', and 'avatar' are not interchangeable translations.

The four/five-world-age schema, vertical cosmologies, migration accounts, and individual names differ across Nahua and Mexica witnesses. This pass does not assert a universal count of heavens or underworld levels.

INAH notes that the Boturini is colonial/incomplete and that pictorial texts work with oral performance; its Aztlan migration account is not literal proof of a single historical itinerary or ethnic origin claim.
sources.evidence_basis: Every character and relationship has a claim-specific primary/critical-witness locator. Getty supplies digitized manuscript folios with Nahuatl transcription and translations; UNAM supplies the cited Leyenda pages; INAH supplies a material/contextual account of the Boturini. This pass is complete only for the declared folios/pages and coverage rule, not for Mexica, Nahua, pre-contact, colonial, regional, or living traditions beyond them; the witnesses are not used as a flattening authority over living Nahua communities.

sources.continuity_scope: Commercial real-time-strategy adaptation, bounded to World's Edge's official launch-era campaign description (4 September 2024) and the officially published Update 19.14612 build (8 June 2026). This pass records only what those first-party witnesses establish about the named Fall of the Trident campaign agents and the game's adaptation mechanics. It is not evidence for Greek, Egyptian, Norse, Atlantean, Chinese, Japanese, Mexica/Aztec, or any other traditional mythic or religious source material.

work_or_witnesses.edition: World's Edge official launch announcement, 4 September 2024; campaign and base-game feature description.
World's Edge official release notes, 8 June 2026; title-screen build 19.14612.

sources.coverage_rule: Include every individually named, non-deity campaign agent expressly identified in the selected official launch campaign description: Arkantos and Gargarensis. Include their directly stated campaign opposition. Gods, pantheons, generic myth and human units, civilizations, resources, technologies, powers, relics, ages, and game modes are retained solely as source terms or character attributes; none becomes a character node. This is deliberately not a roster of all named campaign, skirmish, Arena of the Gods, expansion, or historical/mythic figures in the game.
omissions: All official-game named campaign agents not expressly identified in the selected launch campaign description, including characters introduced or specified only in other campaigns, DLC, Arena of the Gods, Gauntlet, scenario scripting, or later first-party materials
All deities, including named major and minor gods; they are source terms and selection/mechanical attributes under the character-only visualization contract
All generic or collectively named units, civilizations, resources, technologies, powers, relics, buildings, maps, ages, and modes
Traditional mythic witnesses and claims about the cultures represented by the game
uncertainties: The launch article identifies Arkantos, Gargarensis, and their central campaign conflict but does not provide a comprehensive named cast, biography, or full quest-by-quest transcript; the narrow inclusion rule prevents inference beyond that evidence.
Update 19.14612 is a dated mechanical snapshot. Balances, costs, rosters, campaigns, and terminology can change in later builds or expansions.
The official game uses mythic names and categories for fictional gameplay. It does not establish traditional genealogy, cult practice, textual canon, or cross-cultural equivalence.
sources.evidence_basis: First-party World's Edge/Age of Empires launch and versioned release-note pages. The launch post directly names the two selected campaign agents and says Arkantos and allies seek to thwart Gargarensis; it also describes the reusable God Power/Favor, unit, technology, and Wonder Age mechanics. Update 19.14612 fixes the version boundary and independently demonstrates that named deities, myth units, heroes, technologies, God Powers, favor costs, and ages function as game categories rather than a traditional-myth authority.

supports: Arjuna says he is Kṛṣṇa's student and asks instruction while confused about dharma.

Arjuna says his delusion is destroyed, doubt removed, and that he will act according to Kṛṣṇa's word.

comparison_cautions: Do not extract dharma, yoga, divine sight, or Arjuna's final resolve into alignment, leveling, spellcasting, or obedience mechanics.
